title: Assignment 2: shortest paths, DSU and a greedy scan
overview: This assignment checks the graph tools from the last modules on judge-style problems. You use Bellman-Ford when edges can be negative, Floyd-Warshall when many pair queries come in, and DSU to count edges that close a cycle. The last problem is a simple one-pass scan for the two tallest lines.

concepts.term: Pick the shortest-path algorithm from the constraints
concepts.explain: One source with negative weights: Bellman-Ford. Up to about 100 nodes with many pair queries: Floyd-Warshall once, then O(1) per query.
If an extra Bellman-Ford pass still improves a distance, a reachable cycle has negative total weight and 'shortest' is meaningless.
When the same pair can appear several times, keep only the cheapest weight in the matrix.
Each edge whose two ends already share a leader is one extra edge beyond a spanning forest. Count those.

concepts.term: Track the top two in one pass
concepts.explain: Keep the index of the largest and second largest values while scanning; when a new largest appears, the old largest becomes second.

concepts.term: Use long long for sums of big weights
concepts.explain: Weights up to 10^9 added along a path overflow `int` quickly.

files.title: Can Go Again? (Bellman-Ford with negative cycle check)
files.what: Directed graph with possibly negative weights. Run Bellman-Ford once from the source; if a negative cycle is found print one line, otherwise answer each destination query.
steps: Store every edge as an `Edge(a, b, c)` in `edge_list`; set all `dis[i] = LLONG_MAX`.
`bellman_ford` sets `dis[source] = 0` and relaxes all edges repeatedly.
A final pass: if any edge can still relax, return `true` (negative cycle).
In `main`, print `Negative Cycle Detected` and stop if needed.
Otherwise for each query `dest`: print 0 for the source, `Not Possible` for `LLONG_MAX`, else `dis[dest]`.
files.input_note: N E, E edges `A B W`, the source, then T and T destinations. This is the judge's Sample 0.
files.output_note: Prints `0 -1 -2 -5 0`, one per line, matching the sample. For node 4: 1->3 (-2) then 3->4 (-3) gives -5; then 4->5 (+5) gives 0 for node 5.
files.watch_out: The relax loop is `for (int i = 1; i < n-1; i++)`, which is only **n-2** passes instead of n-1. It works on the sample by luck. With input `4 3 / 3 4 1 / 2 3 1 / 1 2 1 / source 1` (edges listed backwards) the program wrongly prints `Negative Cycle Detected`. Fix: `for (int i = 1; i <= n-1; i++)`.

check.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need n-1 passes in the worst case?
check.a: A shortest path can have n-1 edges, and if the edges are listed in the worst order each pass only fixes one more edge of that path.

files.title: Shortest Distance (Floyd-Warshall with queries)
files.what: N is at most 100 but there are up to 10^5 queries, so compute all pairs once with Floyd-Warshall and answer each query from the table.
steps: Fill `adj_mat` for 1..N: 0 on the diagonal, `LLONG_MAX` elsewhere.
For each edge keep the minimum weight, because repeated edges are allowed.
`floyd_warshall` runs the `k`, `i`, `j` loops with the infinity guard.
For each query `X Y` print `adj_mat[X][Y]`, or -1 if it is still infinite.
files.input_note: N E, E edges, Q, then Q queries. This is the judge's Sample 1 (note the repeated edge 1->2).
files.output_note: Prints `4 6 8 2 4 6`, matching the sample. `1 2` is 4, not 10, because the cheaper copy of the edge is kept. `2 1` is 6 via 2->3->1.

check.q: Why not run Dijkstra for every query instead?
check.a: With 10^5 queries that is far too slow. Floyd-Warshall costs about 10^6 steps once for N = 100, and each query is then a lookup.

files.title: Cycle of Edges (DSU)
files.what: Counts the edges that would close a cycle: for every edge, if both ends already share a leader add 1, otherwise union them.
steps: For each edge find both leaders.
files.input_note: N E, then E edges. This is the judge's Sample 0.
files.output_note: Prints `3`. The first four edges form a path joining all 5 nodes; each of the last three edges joins nodes that are already connected.
files.watch_out: `memset(group_size, 1, ...)` sets each byte to 1, not each int. The answer is unaffected, but use a loop to set sizes to 1. A shortcut: the answer is always E - (N - number of components).

check.q: A connected graph has 6 nodes and 9 edges. How many edges close a cycle?
check.a: 9 - 5 = 4, because a spanning tree of 6 nodes uses 5 edges.

files.title: Water (two tallest lines)
files.what: The container is measured only by height, and the water level is the shorter of the two lines. So the best pair is simply the two tallest lines; print their indices left first.
steps: `max1` starts at index 0, `max2` at -1 (no second yet).
For each `i` from 1: if `arr[i]` beats `arr[max1]`, the old best moves to `max2` and `i` becomes `max1`.
Else if there is no `max2` yet or `arr[i]` beats `arr[max2]`, set `max2 = i`.
Return `{min(max1, max2), max(max1, max2)}` so the left index comes first.
files.complexity: Time O(N) per test · Space O(N)
files.input_note: T, then for each test N and the heights. This is the judge's Sample 0.
files.output_note: Prints `1 5` (heights 8 and 7) and `0 3` (heights 5 and 6), matching the sample.
files.watch_out: Don't confuse this with LeetCode's 'Container With Most Water', where width also counts and you need two pointers. Here only height matters.

check.q: Heights `3 9 4 9`? (Suppose heights could repeat.) Which pair would this code print?
check.a: `1 3`: index 1 becomes `max1`, then index 3 is not strictly bigger, so it becomes `max2`.

recap: Read the constraints first: they tell you which shortest-path algorithm fits.
Bellman-Ford needs **n-1** relax passes plus one check pass; an off-by-one breaks it on unlucky edge orders.
Keep the cheapest of repeated edges.
Cycle-making edges = edges whose ends already share a DSU leader.
Finding the top two values needs only one pass and two indices.

check_yourself.q: Negative weights, 1000 nodes, one source. Which algorithm?
check_yourself.a: Bellman-Ford (Dijkstra fails with negative weights; Floyd-Warshall would be 10^9 steps).

check_yourself.q: In Floyd-Warshall, what does `LLONG_MAX` in the final table mean?
check_yourself.a: There is no path from that row's node to that column's node.

check_yourself.q: Why does `dis` need to be `long long` in Can Go Again?
check_yourself.a: Weights reach 10^9 in size, and a path of many edges can go beyond the `int` range in either direction.
